To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pH regulatory systems known for animal cells are absent in Tetrahymenas, but that an amiloride- and Na+-sensitive pH regulatory system can be activated by low concentrations of Cu2+ ions.

1) the Na+/H exchange system is inactive (or absent?) under normal conditions, but can be activated by low concentrations of the metal salt CuSO(4), 2) the Na+/Ca exchange system is present and active, and 3) the Na+-driven lactate transporter is present and active.
Tetrahymena has no active Na+/H+ exchanger and no active H+-ATPase, but that a quiescent Na+/ H+ exchanger can be activated by CuSO4.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pH regulation in the protozoan Tetrahypena pyriformes.
the regulation of intracellular pH in eukaryotic cells.
the mechanisms of acid extrusion in the ciliate protozoan Tetrahumena pyriformi.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Na+/H+-exchanger of Tetrahymena is activated in the presence of Cu2+.
Tetrahymena cells possess the following transport systems: (1) a Na+/H+ exchanger, (2) a lactate transporter, and (3) a Cu2+ transporter.
Tetrahymena cells possess an amiloride- sensitive Na+/H+ exchanger, but that this exchanger is silent under normal conditions and is only activated by low concentrations of Cu2+.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Na+/H + antiport system is present, silent, but can be activated by low concentrations of Cu2+ ions in Tetrahymenapyriformis, and is not involved in pH regulation under normal conditions.
Tetrahymena has a Na+/H+ exchanger that can be activated by Cu2+, but that it has no other known pH regulatory systems, and that it is unable to maintain a stable intracellular pH at pHo 6.8.
Tetrahymena cells have an active Na+/H+ exchanger which can be activated by CuSO4, but no Na+-HCO3– or Na+/OH– exchange systems, and no H+/lactate or H+/ammonium transport systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Na+/H+-exchanger is a very important mechanism for pH homeostasis in Tetrahymema.
the heavy metal salt, copper sulfate, is an effective activator of the Na+/ H+ exchange system in Tetrahymenapyriformis.
we can now use the Tetrahymena system to investigate the mechanism by which the heavy metal salt, CuSO4, activates a quiescent Na+/ H+ exchanger.
